card.title: One good trait casts a halo

body.claim: A positive impression in one area can make a person look better in unrelated areas too.
body.why: This is the halo effect, a term coined by Edward Thorndike. In 1920 he had commanding officers rate soldiers on physical, intellectual, leadership and personal qualities, and found that the correlations between traits were too high and too even. The reverse exists too: negative impressions can spill over, sometimes called the horn effect.

probes.question: What does the halo effect describe?
options: A good impression in one area colouring other judgments
Judging people only by their words

probes.question: True or false: the halo effect only works in a positive direction.

claims.claim: Halo effect: a term coined by Edward Thorndike; positive impression in one area influences opinion in another
claims.quote: a term coined by Edward Thorndike, is the tendency for positive impressions of a person

claims.claim: Halo effect is the tendency for positive impressions in one area to positively influence opinion in another (probe 1)
claims.quote: the tendency for positive impressions of a person, company, country, brand, or product in one area to positively influence one's opinion
it was only officially recognized in 1920 with empirical evidence provided by the psychologist Edward Thorndike

claims.claim: He had commanding officers rate soldiers on physical, intellectual, leadership and personal qualities
claims.quote: Thorndike asked two commanding officers to evaluate their soldiers in terms of physical qualities

claims.claim: He found the correlations too high and too even
claims.quote: The correlations are too high and too even.

claims.claim: Negative impressions can spill over: the horn effect (probe 2: not only positive)
claims.quote: A negative form of the halo effect, called the horn effect, the devil effect, or the reverse halo effect
